summary: Specifies an adaptation layer that provides a lower layer service for DDP over SCTP. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5043 defines how Direct Data Placement can use SCTP as its reliable transport. It specifies how streams pair, how chunks are numbered, and how a DDP session starts and ends.

questions: how does ddp work over sctp
subtitle: Defines how DDP segments and sessions use SCTP streams and data chunks.

tldr.problem: Direct Data Placement needs a reliable lower-layer transport, but the use of SCTP for that service needs defined stream, sequencing and session rules.
tldr.mechanism: The adaptation pairs like-numbered SCTP streams, carries each DDP segment in an unordered data chunk with a DDP-SSN, and uses control chunks to initiate, accept, reject and terminate sessions.
tldr.outcome: It specifies a subset of SCTP that can be implemented over existing stacks or optimized for DDP. RFC 5043 has been updated by RFC 6581 and RFC 7146.

today: RFC 5043 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2007. It has been updated by RFC 6581 and RFC 7146, and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What the Adaptation Layer Provides
sections.content:
Direct Data Placement (DDP) moves data directly to registered memory locations. It needs a reliable lower-layer protocol. RFC 5043 defines an adaptation layer that provides this service using the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP).

The rules specify the subset of SCTP needed to carry DDP and are intended to work over existing SCTP stacks. An implementation may combine the adaptation layer with SCTP for performance, without changing SCTP behavior for other uses.
sections.plainLanguage: DDP needs a reliable way to carry its data segments. This RFC defines how SCTP can provide that transport service.

sections.title: Pairing SCTP Streams
sections.content:
One DDP stream uses a pair of SCTP streams with the same stream identifier, one for each direction. The pair connects two DDP endpoints within an SCTP association.

Each DDP segment is carried in a single unordered SCTP Data Chunk. The adaptation layer adds a DDP Source Stream Sequence Number (DDP-SSN) that records the order in which DDP submitted segments, even though SCTP may deliver unordered chunks in a different order.
sections.plainLanguage: Two SCTP streams with the same identifier form one two-way DDP stream. Each segment carries a DDP-SSN so the receiver can recover submission order even when chunks arrive out of order.

sections.title: Data and Control Chunk Formats
sections.content:
The association signals DDP support with an Adaptation Indication in an INIT or INIT-ACK. The assigned DDP indication is 0x00000001. An association that negotiates this indication carries only the data chunks defined for this adaptation; applications needing both DDP and ordinary SCTP traffic to the same host need separate associations.

The payload protocol identifier distinguishes DDP Segment Chunks (16) from DDP Stream Session Control messages (17). Both contain a DDP-SSN. Control messages also carry a function code and may carry private data. Initiate, Accept and Reject messages include private data, which can be empty but MUST NOT exceed 512 bytes. Terminate messages carry no private data.
sections.plainLanguage: The adaptation marks an SCTP association as DDP and identifies whether a chunk carries a segment or session control. Control messages can include up to 512 bytes of private data, except Terminate messages.

sections.title: Starting and Ending a DDP Session
sections.content:
A session begins when the active endpoint sends Initiate. The passive endpoint can Accept or, at the upper layer's direction, Reject. After acceptance, either endpoint may send DDP segments with increasing DDP-SSNs. At least one endpoint MUST send Terminate to end the session.

The DDP-SSN restarts at zero for each session and MUST have no gaps. Control messages must not be sent if they could arrive before earlier control messages in that session. A stream identifier cannot be reused while a chunk from its previous session may still be in flight.
sections.plainLanguage: An endpoint initiates a session, and its peer accepts or rejects it. After acceptance, the endpoints exchange numbered segments and at least one side sends a termination message.

sections.title: Stream Limits, Fragmentation and Setup
sections.content:
All data chunks MUST use SCTP's unordered option. The receiver must not infer DDP segment order from SCTP transmission sequence numbers. The association must start with equal numbers of inbound and outbound streams, and the adaptation should request the number of streams it may need.

The adaptation tells DDP its maximum segment size. That size is the largest value avoiding IP or SCTP fragmentation, or 516 bytes, whichever is larger. SCTP data-chunk fragmentation MUST NOT be used unless the alternative is IP fragmentation. At setup, each endpoint checks the peer's adaptation indication before using DDP procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The adaptation uses unordered chunks and carries its own ordering number. It also tells DDP the largest segment it can accept and checks that the peer negotiated DDP.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Direct placement into memory can create security risks without adequate local controls. The RFC points to the DDP, RDMA and DDP/RDMA security specifications for those threats and says this adaptation adds no security risks beyond SCTP.

For Remote Direct Data Placement over SCTP, an implementation of IPsec MUST support functionality equivalent to the IPsec support required for TCP by RFC 3723. It SHOULD support the same level for SCTP and TCP unless TCP is not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Direct memory placement requires local security controls. The RFC requires IPsec support for SCTP at the level specified for TCP in the referenced profile.

messages.label: Initiate
messages.note: The session begins with DDP-SSN zero.

messages.label: DDP segments
messages.note: Zero or more segments with increasing DDP-SSNs.
